title: The eight who receive
hookLine: the Qur'an names who zakat is for: the poor, the needy, debtors, travelers and others (9:60)

lines: THE NUMBER IS READY. NOW WHAT?
NOT JUST GIVE: HERE'S THE LIST.
cards: You've worked out the number: two and a half percent, ready to go. Now what? Hand it to the first person who asks?
Drop it in any collection box? Give it to your cousin who's always broke? Most giving is left to the giver's judgment.
Zakat is unusual. The Qur'an doesn't just say give. It gives you the list.
One verse, in Surah at-Tawbah, names exactly who zakat is for. Eight kinds of people. Eight addresses.

teach.b: Chapter nine, verse sixty. In Pickthall's translation it begins: The alms are only for the poor and the needy. Here are all eight.
One, the poor, al-fuqara'. Two, the needy, al-masakin. Scholars differ on which of the two is worse off, but together they're the people who can't cover the basics.

Three, the workers who collect and manage zakat, paid from it so the system runs. Four, those whose hearts are to be reconciled: people new to Islam, or whose goodwill the community needs. Five, to free the captives.
In the Prophet's time that meant helping enslaved people buy their freedom; some scholars today apply it to freeing people from captivity and trafficking.
Six, the debtors, crushed by debts taken on for a decent reason. Seven, in the cause of Allah.
Classically this meant those fighting in defense of the community; some modern scholars read it more widely, for example for education and dawah, and others keep it narrow.
Eight, the wayfarer, stranded far from home, even if rich back there. The verse ends: a duty from Allah. Notice what the list doesn't name: the mosque's new carpet, or the giver's own family.
The jurists say zakat isn't paid to your own parents or children, because you already owe them support.

teach.h: FROM THEIR RICH TO THEIR POOR.
teach.b: Bukhari reports that when the Prophet ﷺ sent Mu'adh to Yemen, he told him to take it from their rich and return it to their poor. Local, specific, human. Zakat doesn't vanish into a fog called charity.

how: Muslims direct their zakat to the eight categories named in 9:60, often through mosques or zakat organizations, preferring local recipients, and not to their own parents or children.

o: a voluntary gift, given whenever you feel moved
a fine paid for missing a prayer
a set share of wealth, owed to eight named groups

games.q: what's inside the eight — tap the pairs.
p: crushed by debts for a decent reason
from their rich to their poor

s: the Qur'an leaves it to each giver to decide who gets zakat
9:60 names eight categories: zakat has addresses.
a stranded traveler can receive zakat even if wealthy at home
the wayfarer is one of the eight, judged by need where they are.
you can pay your zakat to your own parents
the jurists say no: you already owe them support, so it doesn't count as zakat.

games.q: you're Mu'adh, sent to govern Yemen. the Prophet ﷺ tells you how to handle zakat. what does he say?
o: take it from their rich and return it to their poor
spend it on the governor's house
games.why: take it from their rich and return it to their poor (Bukhari 1395). local, specific, human.

practice: Count the eight on your fingers, slowly, and give each a real face: the poor, the needy, the one who collects, a heart being welcomed, a captive, someone drowning in debt, the cause of Allah, a traveler stranded at a station at midnight.
Go through them twice, and notice which face stays with you longest.

wordCard.voice: Zakat, given to the eight kinds of people Surah at-Tawbah names: the poor, the needy, the workers, reconciled hearts, captives, debtors, the cause of Allah, and the traveler.

orig.note: Arabic: the alms are only for the poor, the opening of 9:60.

carryVoice: Your line: it has addresses. Eight fingers, eight faces, eight kinds of people. See you tomorrow.
